candidates.title: 5 days beneath the waves: What it's like to live in an underwater 'space station'
candidates.raw_excerpt: Living underwater was surprisingly peaceful. It was in many ways exactly what I imagine living on Mars would be like one day. There were no humans around us, except for my three SEA STAR crewmembers and me. Apart from the human noises we made, we couldn't hear anything other than the life support systems keeping us alive submerged 22 feet (7 meters) below the surface. We were living in these extreme conditions to study the challenges astronauts may face on long-duration space missions. Since performing research in space is still rare and expensive, there are numerous facilities around the world that focus on recreating space-like conditions on Earth . One of those stations is the Jules' Undersea Lab, where the SEA STAR simulated space mission took place. This underwater habitat was called "La Chalupa" when it was built in the 1970s. Its purpose was to allow divers to live and perform research as aquanauts — people who spend more than 24 hours underwater in a so-called state of saturation. Today, the Jules' Undersea Lab is located near Key Largo, in Florida. However, it was originally designed to be mobile — inside a barge 20 feet wide and 60 feet long (6 to 18 meters). The SEA STAR crew inside the Jules' Undersea Lab, as seen from the outside of the station by a member of Mission Control. (Image credit: Ozlem Berg) The aquanauts could choose an ideal site for their research expeditions underwater and then have the facility be submerged. They did that by flooding most of its inside space, turning it from a boat to a submarine. Once their work was done, they could remove the water and move "La Chalupa" to another location. Unfortunately, the funding to keep this facility running ran out over time, and it was moved one last time to its current home. candidates.raw_excerpt: Rendezvous Robotics has shifted its focus to spacecraft that can autonomously build themselves in orbit. The company announced a $20 million seed round on Wednesday, staking a plan to demonstrate a self-assembling and re-assembling spacecraft in orbit in 2028. Rendezvous Robotics came out of stealth last year to commercialize modular self-assembly TESSERAE technology developed by co-founder Dr. Ariel Ekblaw at MIT. The company started out focused on in-space assembly of large phased array antennas, solar panels, in-space manufacturing sites, and future space habitats. Co-founder and CEO Joe Landon tells Via Satellite this in-space assembly technology can meet the urgent need for missions like remote sensing and communications for both commercial and government. “Large habitats and space stations [are] all still very much in our vision for the company. But we’ve decided to focus on the missions that we know there is an acute need for today — for more performance and more flexible spacecraft,” he said. Landon and Rendezvous want to challenge satellite operators to think beyond the launch fairing. What if satellites didn’t have to be designed to fold up inside a fairing? “Instead of spending time and money and energy designing systems to be intricately folded up and to survive launch in that folded up form, send the parts to space and build there,” Landon says. “It’s a simple concept — but having to fit every satellite into a rocket is a ridiculous constraint that we cannot tolerate going forward.” The company’s core technology is a stealth assembly system, made up of hexagonal tiles about 3 feet in diameter. The tiles use electromagnets to maneuver and physically latch together to establish a power and data connection. candidates.title: The last, best hope for space tourism just rolled onto a runway in Arizona
candidates.raw_excerpt: The private space tourism era looked so very promising five years ago. Blue Origin and Virgin Galactic had begun flying customers—real people with zero space experience—on suborbital missions. And at about the same time, private citizens were going to orbit for days at a time aboard SpaceX's Crew Dragon. But that was then. Consider the state of play today: It has been 10 months since Blue Origin's New Shepard spacecraft flew its last mission in January. The program was subsequently "paused," but let's be real. Blue Origin has moved on. New Shepard's engineering teams are now supporting the New Glenn rocket and Blue Moon lander programs. SpaceX flew its final free-flyer mission on Dragon, Fram2, in April 2025. A handful of non-NASA missions bound for space stations remain on the spacecraft's manifest, but all are likely to carry at least one government astronaut. Then Dragon will be retired. candidates.title: Black holes can split in two — but only if they spin at extreme speeds
candidates.raw_excerpt: Scientists have long known that when two black holes collide, they merge to create a more massive black hole. These events are so violent that they set the very fabric of space ringing with ripples called gravitational waves. Now, new research suggests that the opposite may happen, too: single black holes may be able to split in two. But this can only happen if that progenitor black hole is spinning at maximum possible speed. That speed prevents the black holes from immediately falling back on each other. There are physical laws in place that would usually prevent black holes from splitting in two; the team behind this research investigated whether there are conditions in which these laws can be temporarily bypassed. One of the key aspects of physics that prevents black holes from bifurcating comes from thermodynamics . Black holes possess a characteristic called " entropy ," which is essentially a measure of disorder within a system. Imagine a toddler's crayon box. When entropy is low, the crayons are neatly arranged by color. As entropy is increased, the crayons are scattered and no longer in order. To get the crayons back in order, it requires a parent to put energy into the system and neatly reorder the crayons. In other words, the entropy of a system can't be reduced without some intervention and energy being added from outside that system. Parenting would be a little easier if it could. A black hole splitting in two would represent a decrease in entropy, strongly disfavored by the laws of thermodynamics, but only if the black hole is not rotating. The situation could be different for a rapidly rotating black hole. This team of scientists found that a loophole exists for such a black hole. candidates.title: How 'spacewalking' underwater made me feel like I was really in space
candidates.raw_excerpt: I was breathing just fine through my life support systems, but I kept feeling an urge to double check that everything was ok with my "spacesuit" before heading out on this "spacewalk." I have worn many different types of spacesuits on Earth during my career, but for the first time in my life, I knew that I couldn’t just stop to breathe the air outside if there were an emergency. That's because I was underwater. On this excursion, I was leading a simulated space mission underwater called SEA STAR. My " spacesuit " was actually scuba diving gear, and the simulated spacewalks , or EVAs (Extra-Vehicular Activities), included outings where we explored underwater environments. Being underwater, if we encountered a major problem with our gear, we would have had to treat it as seriously as if we were astronauts on the International Space Station . There was no immediate "out." This was serious. Before this underwater mission, I had worked as the commander of nearly 40 analog missions that simulated crewed missions to the moon and Mars . The goal of these types of missions is to test what living and working in lunar or Martian environments might be like. We study everything from the psychology of living in extreme conditions, or in isolation, to the technology that astronauts might use to complete those missions successfully. Testing spacesuit technology is also an important part of these analog space missions. These suits are usually a much simpler version of the ones astronauts use in space, which can weigh around 310 pounds (141 kilograms) when fully equipped with life support systems. Analog spacesuits usually weigh a maximum of 30 pounds (14 kg). While there are many differences between suits designed for use in space and these suits designed for testing on Earth , the biggest one is that, on an analog mission, crew members can open their helmets and breathe the outside air if necessary. candidates.title: Airbus and Thales Contracted for 2 Galileo Satellites Each
candidates.raw_excerpt: The European Space Agency (ESA) awarded contracts this week to both Airbus and Thales Alenia Space contracts to build two additional Galileo satellites each to enhance the Galileo navigation system. This contract means that each manufacturer will now build eight second generation Galileo (G2) satellites. ESA previously contracted both manufacturers in 2021 for six G2 satellites each. ESA stated the four satellites are scheduled for delivery in 2031 will launch soon after. They will be identical to the G2 satellites already under development. They will be equipped with fully digital navigation payloads, inter-satellite link capacity and an advanced atomic clock configuration, with more reliable positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) services. “With these contracts, ESA and European industry are safeguarding the continuity of Europe’s satellite navigation services, responding to the evolving needs of users, and strengthening Europe’s strategic autonomy. These contracts represent an investment in Europe’s ability to navigate its own future, independently and with confidence,” commented ESA Director of Resilience, Navigation and Connectivity Laurent Jaffart. The Galileo system has been in operation since 2016 and is currently composed of 36 satellites in orbit, with two remaining to launch. The 16-satellite G2 system will join the first generation and continue the constellation and support new services. ESA reports that development and qualification activities are nearing completion for the first 12 G2 satellites, which are set to begin launching in 2028. candidates.title: Astronomers discover the secrets of 'string of pearls' supernova relic and the zombie star at its heart
candidates.raw_excerpt: Scientists are still learning about a cosmic "string of pearls," a unique celestial relic left by a supernova explosion that humanity witnessed around 850 years ago. That is thanks to the most detailed observation of the dandelion-shaped chains of gas and supernova debris that comprise Pa 30, the only supernova remnant of its type observed in the Milky Way . What makes Pa 30 even more unique is that it has a rare "zombie star" at its heart. Supernovas like the one that created Pa 30 are called Type Ia supernovas; they happen when a dead star called a white dwarf overfeeds on a companion star like a cosmic vampire. This overfeeding triggers a runaway nuclear explosion that usually destroys the white dwarf. But on rare occasions, the supernova doesn't completely destroy the star, and a shattered stellar body remains, called a zombie star. These events are called Type Iax supernovas . Pa 30 was first identified in 2013 by a citizen scientist in 2013, but scientists soon linked it to a cosmic explosion recorded independently in the year 1181 in Japanese, Chinese, and Arabic historical documentation. That makes this one of only five supernovas seen before the invention of the telescope. "Reliable historical records of stellar explosions extend back only about a thousand years. For all we know, there might well be similar remnants still lurking in the dark in our own galaxy," team member Ilaria Caiazzo, assistant professor at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA), said in a statement . "Today, we are lucky to study an intriguing object we know was observed by astronomers who made three independent historical records of the event centuries before the invention of the telescope." Solar system-sized pearls Pa 30 is a good laboratory to study supernovas because, at around 7,500 light-years away, it is relatively close to Earth on cosmic scales. candidates.title: November full moon 2026: When, where and how to see the Beaver Moon
candidates.raw_excerpt: The November full moon reaches maximum illumination at 9:53 a.m. EST (1453 GMT) on Nov. 24, as the lunar disk sits opposite the sun in Earth's sky, appearing fully lit by its rays. November's full moon is traditionally known as the " Beaver Moon ", because it rises around the time when the small mammals take refuge in their dens, having stored enough food to survive the long winter months, according to the Old Farmer's Almanac . The Nov. 24 full moon also happens to be the first of three consecutive " supermoons ". The non-scientific term is often bestowed on full moons that occur when the natural satellite is within 90% of perigee, when the moon is closest to Earth in its elliptical orbit. The proximity can make a supermoon appear 14% larger and 30% brighter than the smallest full moon of the year, according to NASA . When to see the November full moon The November full moon will be below the horizon for stargazers in the U.S. when it turns full at 9:53 a.m. EST on Nov. 24. Instead, viewers in America will get their best view of the near-full Beaver Moon as it arcs towards the western horizon in the predawn hours of Nov. 23. You may notice the lunar disk take on a gorgeous yellow-orange hue in the hour before moonset, as the bluer wavelengths of its light are scattered by Earth's dense atmosphere through a process known as Rayleigh scattering — the same phenomenon that turns the sky red at sunset. candidates.title: ESA’s INVICTUS Hypersonic Programme Clears First Major Review
candidates.raw_excerpt: Credit: Frazer-Nash The European Space Agency’s (ESA) INVICTUS hypersonic aircraft programme has cleared its first major requirements review and moved into the next phase of development, with a second review expected in October 2027. Stephan Carroll, INVICTUS chief engineer at Frazer-Nash, confirmed on LinkedIn on 23 October that the programme had successfully completed its first System Requirements Review (SRR-1) in March 2026. According to Carroll, the company held back on announcing the milestone “while subsequent programme planning activities were agreed with ESA and UKSA.” “With the next phase Kick-Off, the programme is on track towards SRR-2, currently planned for October 2027,” Carroll wrote. According to Carroll, work on the aircraft’s design has progressed across several areas, including aerodynamics, propulsion, pre-cooling, systems engineering, safety, certification and cost modelling. Frazer-Nash was awarded a €7 million ESA contract in July 2025 to conduct the initial design work for the INVICTUS programme. Through the programme, ESA aims to develop a reusable hypersonic test aircraft capable of reaching Mach 5. In its original procurement documents, ESA envisaged a Mach 5 flight by 2028. However, when Frazer-Nash formally announced the programme in July 2025, the company was targeting the first flight of a Mach 5-capable aircraft in early 2031. In June 2026, ESA’s INVICTUS technical lead, David Perigo, indicated that the programme was expected to be well into integrated propulsion testing by around 2032, suggesting that the aircraft’s first flight may have been pushed back by at least a year, potentially longer. candidates.title: What causes mysterious long delayed radio echoes in Earth's atmosphere?
candidates.raw_excerpt: In 1927, Norwegian civil engineer and amateur radio operator Jørgen Hals made an unusual discovery: while monitoring transmissions from a shortwave radio station in Eindhoven, The Netherlands, he began hearing odd, "delayed" radio echoes, arriving approximately three seconds after the original transmissions, that sometimes accompanied the station's signals. "From where this echo comes I cannot say for the present," Hals wrote of his peculiar discovery, adding that he could "only confirm that I really heard it." Almost a century after Hals' discovery, the exact cause of this unusual phenomenon — known today as long delayed echoes, or LDEs — remains unknown. Their baffling nature has prompted a range of potential explanations, most of which focus on a variety of unexplained natural phenomena occurring in Earth's atmosphere . However, a few more far-out possibilities, including potential evidence of extraterrestrial technology, have also been considered. What do we know? A curious discovery The enigma of long-delayed echoes has perplexed scientists since their initial detection by Hals, who at the time reported his odd findings to Norwegian physicist Carl Størmer. candidates.raw_excerpt: As tech billionaires make bank off an AI trade that now threatens retirement accounts and university endowments , a criminal element is rising to take advantage of the crumbs that fall off the table. Another truckload bound for Texas went missing in a similar fashion, with a $10 million server rack vanishing after the escort vehicle was rammed and its GPS tracker manipulated by an unknown actor. “The accident was not an accident,” private cargo theft investigator Gerardo Pachuca told NBC . “The bad guys wanted that load, so they intentionally took out the escorts.” As various tech industry leaders and investigators told the publication, thefts of AI data center equipment in transit has resulted in over $100 million in losses since June of 2026 alone. Since last year, NBC identified some two dozen cargo thefts of components across the US, a number that’s expected to grow as the data center boom continues. Keith Lewis, head of operations at risk-management firm Verisk CargoNet told NBC that it’s “like stealing pure gold bars.” “We’ve seen some of these thefts go up into 30-plus million dollars for one particular shipment,” Lewis continued. “It’s so much easier to steal this than to rob a bank.” More on data centers: Wolves Descend on Finnish Villages After Google Hacked Down 1,300 Acres of Habitat to Make Room for AI Data Centers The post Thieves Are Making a Fortune Heisting AI Data Center Equipment appeared first on Futurism .

Cassini completed its first flyby on July 3, 2004, but when it swung by a second time on Oct. 26, it got about 300 times closer than it did the first time. At the closest point of this flyby, Cassini was 745 miles (1,200 kilometers) away from the surface of Titan. The spacecraft took hundreds of photos during this flyby , and these were the highest resolution views of Titan anyone had ever seen. It included bright features that hinted at a mountain range, as well as a large basin and smooth plains regions. candidates.title: NASA ends Swift space telescope mission after failed rescue attempt
candidates.raw_excerpt: NASA has officially ended the mission of its Swift space telescope, after a private satellite failed in its bold bid to rescue the aging spacecraft. That rescue mission was led by the Arizona company Katalyst Space Technologies, whose LINK spacecraft tried to meet up with Swift this summer to boost its orbit. That didn't work out, however, so Swift continues its fall back toward Earth. The telescope is expected to reenter Earth's atmosphere "in the next few weeks," NASA said in a statement on Friday (Oct. 23). That statement served primarily to announce the end of the Swift mission after more than 20 very productive years. The telescope launched to Earth orbit in November 2004, tasked with studying gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) — the most powerful explosions in the cosmos. Swift was designed to operate for two years, but it continued studying the high-energy universe for more than two decades. "In that time, Swift played a major role in advancing our understanding of the changing universe and was part of a revolution in astrophysics that showed how critical rapid-response observations are to the entire community," Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of the Astrophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington, said in the statement. NASA had hoped to keep Swift going even longer. In September 2025, the agency awarded a contract to the Arizona company Katalyst Space Technologies to rescue the observatory, which was falling back to Earth thanks to atmospheric drag. Swift has no thrusters capable of counteracting this drag. So Katalyst built a refrigerator-sized spacecraft called LINK, which aimed to rendezvous with Swift, grapple it with three robotic arms and boost it to a higher orbit, allowing the observatory to continue its science work. NASA and Katalyst stressed from the start that success was far from guaranteed. After all, LINK's mission was unprecedented: No private spacecraft had ever captured and boosted a satellite that wasn't designed to be serviced in this way.
